title: MIT Students Build a Robot in 3 Days—and It Actually Worked!
summary:
What would you do if your robot stopped working right before a big show? A team of MIT students faced that exact problem at the Governors Cup, a giant robotics tournament for high schoolers. Their robot, Timbot, had Wi-Fi troubles. So they sat on the floor, pulled out a long Ethernet cable, and got to work. Soon, a crowd of high school students gathered around, asking questions. "We ended up tethering the robot with a long Ethernet cable, instead of using wireless, and a lot of students were like, 'whoa, we do that too!'" said Lily Sand, a first-year student. It turned into a perfect connection moment.

These MIT students are part of a new club called FIRSTxMIT. They all grew up doing FIRST Robotics, a program that teaches kids to build robots and work as a team. At MIT, about one in five students did FIRST in high school! The club wants to share that excitement with more kids. They even built Timbot in just three days during a challenge called Robot in 3 Days. That's way faster than the six weeks it usually takes a high school team.

At the Governors Cup, the team showed off Timbot, chatted with students, and even talked to governors about why STEM education matters. Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey stopped by to show her support. The club plans to keep spreading the robot love, maybe even helping more schools start their own teams. As club co-founder Perry Han says, "We want to put a robot in as many students' hands as possible."
why_it_matters: Even smart college students still use simple fixes like a cable, and you can join a robotics club too—building stuff with friends is for everyone.

background_read: MIT (the Massachusetts Institute of Technology) is a world-famous university where students invent all kinds of technology.
FIRST Robotics is a huge program started in 1989 to get kids excited about building robots. Each year, thousands of teams have just six weeks to create a robot for a game challenge.
The Governors Cup is a special tournament where top high school teams show off their robots and meet important leaders.
Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey is the leader of the state where MIT is located.
Article_Structure: WHO: A new MIT student club called FIRSTxMIT, co-founded by students like Perry Han.
WHAT: They built a robot named Timbot in only three days, then fixed a Wi-Fi problem with an Ethernet cable at the Governors Cup.
WHERE: At the Governors Cup robotics tournament, where high school teams competed.
WHY: To share the excitement of STEM and help more students get a chance to build robots.

perspectives.description: Getting to see a working robot up close makes science feel real and fun. Students might think, 'If they did it in three days, maybe I can do it in six weeks.'

Building a robot super-fast is exciting, but some teachers might worry that rushing could lead to mistakes or broken parts. Still, the team showed that quick building teaches creative problem-solving.
To the MIT students, this was never about the perfect robot. It was about showing that robotics is not just for experts—any high schooler can jump in, make mistakes, and still have a working machine.
